title: Dying at Maghar
hook: believing the holy city promised no special freedom, Kabir went to die at Maghar, a place thought unlucky (Kabir, Gauri)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Loi: Kabir speaking his hymns across the room, at home. Your line was saints live in homes.

Some places carry a promise. Pilgrims in Kabir's world believed that whoever died in Kashi, the holy city of Benares, would be set free. Another town, Maghar, had the opposite reputation: die there, people said, and your next birth would be a poor one. Kabir lived his whole life in Kashi. Then, near the end, by his own account in a hymn, he got up and went to Maghar.
screen: `KASHI — THE CITY OF THE PROMISE.` → `MAGHAR — THE UNLUCKY TOWN.` → `KABIR GETS UP AND GOES.`

segments.voice: The hymn is in Raag Gauri, on Ang 326. Its turn, in paraphrase: my whole life I spent in Shiva's city, and at the time of death I rose and came to Maghar. Then the sharp question. If Kabir leaves his body in Kashi, what favor would he owe the Lord? If the city does the saving, the Lord has nothing left to do. A promise tied to a place sounds generous, but it quietly moves freedom out of the heart and onto a map. Kabir refuses the trade. He'd rather owe everything to the Lord than owe it to an address. In another hymn he puts it flatly, in paraphrase: to one who has the Lord in the heart, Kashi and Maghar are the same. So the walk to Maghar isn't a stunt. It's the hymn acted out. And Kabir doesn't mock the pilgrims or call the holy city bad. He says it isn't the thing that saves. A place can be dear, can help you remember, can be full of people praying. Sikhs travel to historic gurdwaras, too. The Gurus taught that the bath that counts is in the Name, not only the water. Some superstitions today are smaller: the lucky shirt, the seat always taken, the step never skipped. They look harmless. Kabir's question still fits them. If the shirt does the work, what's left for you, and what's left for God?
screen: `MY WHOLE LIFE IN SHIVA'S CITY.` · `WHAT FAVOR WOULD I OWE THE LORD?` · `KASHI AND MAGHAR, THE SAME.` · `THE LUCKY SHIRT, THE SAME QUESTION.` · then, large: `THE PLACE DOESN'T SAVE YOU.`

segments.voice: Let your mind look for one small habit kept for luck, if you have one: a seat, the order of your morning, a number you avoid; if none comes, take any fixed habit. Just notice it, without scolding, and picture doing it the other way once, feeling what's left when the charm is gone. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out.
Maghar. The town thought unlucky to die in, where Kabir went at the end, because the place doesn't do the saving.
Your line: the place doesn't save you. With the Lord in the heart, Kashi and Maghar are the same. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Sikhs read Kabir's Maghar hymn as part of Gurbani, and Sikh teaching holds that liberation comes through the Name and grace, not through dying in a particular holy place.
